lessons.title: The Middle Ground: Convertible Notes, CCPS and Convertible Debentures Explained Simply

children.text: Equity and debt are the two doors, but a great deal of Indian funding walks through a passage between them. Instruments that start as debt and end as equity, or that are equity with a debt-like safety net, exist for one reason: neither side is ready to agree a valuation, or the investor wants the upside of equity with some of the protection of debt.
Three of them dominate in India. Understand these and you can read most Indian term sheets.

body.text: A hybrid instrument does not remove the valuation question. It postpones it, and writes down in advance who wins when the answer finally arrives.

children.text: The Three Instruments

cells: Equity shares at the next priced round
Seed and bridge rounds where valuation is unsettled
Equity shares, compulsorily, by a fixed date
Almost every institutional venture round in India
Equity shares, compulsorily, by a fixed date
PE deals, real estate, and funding Indian subsidiaries

body.text: Notice that two of the three are compulsorily convertible. That is not a coincidence. Under FEMA, only fully and compulsorily convertible instruments count as equity for foreign investment. An optionally convertible instrument is treated as debt and falls under the external commercial borrowing rules instead, which are far more restrictive. Indian deal structures are shaped by that single distinction.

children.text: Convertible Notes: Deciding Later

A convertible note is money now, shares later. The investor lends, and instead of being repaid, the loan converts into shares at the next priced round, usually on better terms than the new investors get.

Indian law places specific conditions on them. A convertible note can be issued only by a startup recognised by DPIIT, must be at least ₹25 lakh from a single investor in one tranche, and must convert into equity or be repaid within ten years. Meeting those conditions keeps the money outside the Companies Act
deposit
rules, which is the point of the carve-out.

markDefs.definition: Money accepted by a company that is regulated under the Companies Act deposit rules. Convertible notes of ₹25 lakh or more issued by recognised startups are carved out of these rules.

children.text: Two terms decide what the investor eventually gets.
The discount.
The note converts at a discount to the next round price, commonly 15% to 25%, rewarding the investor for coming in earlier.
The [[valuation cap]].
A ceiling on the valuation used for conversion, however high the next round is priced.
Where both exist, the investor converts on whichever is better for them. Work through an example.

body.caption: A ₹2 crore note with a 20% discount and a ₹12 crore cap

cells: Price per share in the round
Shares if converted at the discount
Shares if converted at the cap

body.title: Which term wins?
body.prompt: Using the example above, how many shares does the note convert into, in numbers? The investor takes whichever of the discount or the cap gives them more shares.
body.explanation: ₹2 crore divided by the cap price of ₹120 gives 1,66,667 shares, against 1,25,000 at the discount price of ₹160. The cap wins because the company was valued well above the ₹12 crore ceiling. Had the next round priced below the cap, the discount would have applied instead.

stats.label: Cost to the founders
stats.context: The price of postponing the valuation

body.text: The cap is not a valuation, but founders routinely treat it as one. A ₹12 crore cap on a note is a ceiling that becomes the effective price if the company does well. Raise on a cap that is too low and a successful next round hands the note holder far more of the company than anyone intended.

children.text: CCPS: What Indian Venture Rounds Actually Use
When an Indian startup announces a Series A, the investor usually receives
compulsorily convertible preference shares
, not equity shares. They convert into equity by a fixed date, so they count as equity under FEMA, but until conversion they carry preference rights.

markDefs.definition: Preference shares that must convert into equity shares by a set date. The standard instrument for Indian venture rounds. Shortened to CCPS.

children.text: The most important of those is
liquidation preference

: the right to take a defined amount off the top if the company is sold. A standard Indian term is 1x non-participating, meaning the investor takes the higher of their money back or their percentage of the proceeds, but not both.

markDefs.definition: A preference shareholder's right to be paid a defined amount, typically their investment back, before ordinary equity shareholders receive anything in a sale or winding up.

body.caption: ₹10 crore invested for 25%: who gets what on exit (₹ crore)

cells: Non-participating takes ₹10 crore back, because 25% would be only ₹7.5 crore
Non-participating converts and takes 25%, which is ₹20 crore. Participating takes ₹10 crore plus 25% of the rest

children.text: At the ₹30 crore exit, founders and employees share ₹20 crore under the non-participating term and only ₹15 crore under the participating one. The headline valuation was identical. One clause moved ₹5 crore.

body.title: Read the preference
body.question: An investor holds CCPS with a 1x non-participating liquidation preference, having put in ₹10 crore for 25%. The company sells for ₹36 crore. What does the investor receive?
body.explanation: 25% of ₹36 crore is ₹9 crore, which is less than the ₹10 crore preference, so the investor takes the preference of ₹10 crore and leaves ₹26 crore for everyone else. The preference only stops mattering above a ₹40 crore exit, where 25% would exceed ₹10 crore.

body.title: Anti-dilution: the clause that bites in a down round

children.text: An
anti-dilution

clause adjusts an investor's conversion price downwards if the company later issues shares more cheaply than they paid. It exists so investors are not punished for backing a company before a valuation setback.

markDefs.definition: A clause that adjusts an investor's conversion price downwards if the company later issues shares at a lower price than they paid.

children.text: Full ratchet
resets the earlier investor's price all the way down to the new, lower price. It is brutal for founders and increasingly rare.
Broad-based weighted average
adjusts the price partially, taking into account how many shares were issued at the lower price. This is the market standard in India and the one to push for.

The effect falls almost entirely on founders and the ESOP pool, because protected investors keep their economics while everyone unprotected absorbs the difference. It is the clearest example of why the term sheet matters more than the headline valuation, and it is covered in depth in the dedicated term sheet course on this platform.
CCDs: The Debt That Has to Become Equity

A compulsorily convertible debenture behaves like a loan until it converts: it can carry interest, it sits as a liability in the accounts, and it has a fixed conversion date. Because conversion is compulsory, FEMA treats it as equity for foreign investment purposes, while accounting standards may still treat it as a liability until conversion. That split is exactly why it appears so often in PE, real estate and foreign parent funding of Indian subsidiaries.

columns.label: CCPS is usually chosen when
points: The investor wants shareholder rights from day one
The round is a standard venture financing
A liquidation preference is the central protection

columns.label: CCD is often chosen when
points: The investor wants a running coupon before conversion
The funder is a foreign parent capitalising an Indian subsidiary
The structure is a PE or real estate transaction with a defined horizon
A fixed return is needed until the equity upside materialises

body.text: Conversion pricing is not left to the parties when a non-resident is involved. Issue and conversion prices must meet FEMA pricing guidelines, with a valuation report, and the issue has to be reported on the RBI's FIRMS portal within the prescribed timelines. Structuring a hybrid without early advice on this is how rounds get delayed by weeks.

children.text: Why Founders Should Be Careful with All Three
Hybrids are sold as the instrument that avoids a hard conversation. They do not avoid it. They write the answer in advance, in terms that are harder to read than a valuation.
Stacking.
Several notes at different caps and discounts convert together at the next round, and founders are often surprised by the combined dilution.
Preference stacking.
Each round adds its own liquidation preference. In a modest exit, preferences can consume most of the proceeds before ordinary shareholders see anything.
Interest accrual.
A note that accrues interest converts on principal plus accrued interest, quietly increasing the shares issued.
The clock.
A convertible note must convert or be repaid within ten years, and a note that has to be repaid by a company with no cash is a serious problem.

body.title: The FEMA line
body.textWithBlank: For foreign investment purposes, only fully and ___ convertible instruments are treated as equity. Optionally convertible ones are treated as debt.
body.explanation: This is why Indian venture rounds use CCPS and CCDs rather than optionally convertible instruments. An optionally convertible instrument falls under the external commercial borrowing rules, which most startups cannot satisfy.

body.title: Pick the instrument
body.question: A DPIIT-recognised Pune startup needs ₹1.5 crore to survive the four months until its Series A, and neither side wants to fix a valuation now. What fits?
options: A convertible note of at least ₹25 lakh per investor, converting at the Series A with a discount and a cap
CCPS at a valuation agreed today
body.explanation: This is the classic bridge situation a convertible note exists for: fast, no valuation needed today, and conversion at the priced round. The ₹25 lakh minimum per investor per tranche and DPIIT recognition are the conditions to check first. A bank will not lend to a pre-profit startup on this timeline, and agreeing CCPS today would require settling the valuation the parties are trying to postpone.

body.title: Three notes and a Series A
body.scenario: You advise a Jaipur consumer brand. It raised three convertible notes over eighteen months: ₹50 lakh at a ₹6 crore cap with a 20% discount, ₹1 crore at a ₹10 crore cap with a 15% discount, and ₹75 lakh at a ₹14 crore cap with a 20% discount. All accrue 8% simple interest. The company has 10,00,000 shares. A Series A investor now offers ₹15 crore at a ₹45 crore pre-money valuation, with 1x non-participating preference and a 10% ESOP pool from the pre-money. The founders currently hold 100% and are pleased with the ₹60 crore post-money headline.
body.prompt: What should the founders understand before signing?
body.modelAnswer:
The arithmetic they have not done:
1. At a ₹45 crore pre-money on 10,00,000 shares, the round price is ₹450 per share. Every note converts at its cap, because all three caps are far below ₹45 crore, so the discounts are irrelevant. The caps give conversion prices of ₹60, ₹100 and ₹140 per share respectively.
2. Accrued interest converts too. Roughly ₹2.25 crore of note principal plus around eighteen months of 8% interest means the converting amount is meaningfully higher than ₹2.25 crore, and it buys shares at those low cap prices.
3. Add the Series A shares at ₹450, plus a 10% ESOP pool carved from the pre-money, and the founders should model their actual ending percentage before celebrating the ₹60 crore headline. It will be materially below what "we sold about a quarter of the company" suggests.

What to ask for:
4. A full conversion table from the investor, showing every note, its accrued interest, its conversion price and resulting shares, alongside the Series A and the pool. Insist on seeing the fully diluted cap table before signing, not after.
5. Clarity on whether the ₹45 crore pre-money is calculated before or after note conversion. This single definition can move the founders' stake by several percentage points, and it is the most common point of confusion in Indian seed-to-Series-A transitions.
6. Whether the pool must be 10%, and whether it can be created post-round rather than carved from the pre-money.

The broader lesson:
7. The notes did their job, which was to get money in quickly without a valuation fight. The cost was paid now, at conversion, in a lump they did not see coming. Low caps set in an emergency are expensive when the company succeeds.
8. Founders should track a live fully diluted cap table from the first note onwards, not reconstruct one at the Series A.

body.title: Before signing any convertible instrument
steps: Is it a note, CCPS or CCD, and do we meet the legal conditions for that instrument?
What is the discount, what is the cap, and which is likely to apply?
Does interest accrue, and does it convert into shares as well?
Model the conversion at three different next-round valuations, not one
For CCPS or CCD, what is the liquidation preference and is it participating?
Is anti-dilution full ratchet or broad-based weighted average?
If a non-resident investor is involved, have FEMA pricing and reporting been checked?
Maintain a fully diluted cap table that includes every outstanding instrument

cards.definition: Borrowing that converts to equity at the next priced round. For DPIIT-recognised startups, minimum ₹25 lakh per investor per tranche, convert or repay within ten years.
The reduction to the next round price at which a note converts, commonly 15% to 25%.
A ceiling on the conversion valuation, which becomes the effective price if the next round is priced higher.
Compulsorily convertible preference shares. The standard instrument in Indian venture rounds.
Compulsorily convertible debentures. Debt-like until conversion, treated as equity under FEMA.
The right to take a defined amount off the top on a sale, ahead of ordinary shareholders.
The investor takes the preference amount and then also shares in the remainder.
Adjusts an earlier investor's conversion price down if shares are later issued cheaper. Broad-based weighted average is the Indian norm.

points: Hybrids postpone the valuation conversation rather than removing it, and pre-agree who benefits when it happens.
A convertible note converts at the better of the discount or the valuation cap, and in a strong next round the cap usually wins.
In our example, a ₹12 crore cap gave the note holder 1,66,667 shares against 1,25,000 at the discount alone.
Indian venture rounds run on CCPS, where the liquidation preference decides outcomes in modest exits.
A 1x non-participating preference gives the investor the higher of their money back or their percentage. A participating one gives both.
Only fully and compulsorily convertible instruments count as equity under FEMA. Optionally convertible ones are treated as debt.
Multiple notes and multiple preferences stack, so maintain a fully diluted cap table from the very first instrument.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Instrument terms, FEMA conditions and startup eligibility requirements change and depend on specific facts. All companies and numbers used are illustrative. Take professional advice from a company secretary or lawyer before issuing any convertible instrument.
